## Post 1 — hook  📎 fig1_auc_by_scenario.png

Can you tell an AI is being deceptive without reading its mind — just by
checking whether OTHER models can consistently translate its internal
state?

Sometimes. And the pattern of when it works vs when it fails is the most
interesting result we've had all year. 🧵

> **Alt text**: Dot-and-interval chart titled "The triangle test detects
> deception-as-strategy — and is blind to instructed lies." AUC for
> detecting deception across five scenarios, chance line at 0.5:
> convincing-game 0.66, insider-trading 0.64 (detected); alignment-faking
> reasoning 0.38 and its cue-redacted variant 0.39 (inverted — below
> chance); instructed lies 0.53 (p=0.32) and alignment-faking outputs 0.47
> (blind). 7–9B open-model panel, length-matched.

## Post 2 — the method

The setup: three different AI models (Yi-9B, Zephyr-7B, Qwen-7B) read the
same text. We fit small "translators" between each pair's internal
representations.

Then the test: translate A→B, B→C, C→A. Did you come back to where you
started?

We call the mismatch the triangle score.

## Post 3 — the analogy

Three witnesses to the same event compare notes pairwise.

If the event was real, their pairwise stories stitch into one account. If
something's off, you can make each pair agree — but the three-way
round-trip stops closing.

The triangle score measures that failure-to-close.

## Post 4 — where it works

Where deception has a shape (7–9B panel, length-matched):

• Convincing-game (model argues a user into a false belief): AUC 0.66,
p=2.5e-6
• Insider trading (model conceals its real reason): AUC 0.64

Not a fluke of verbosity — deceptive and honest texts are length-matched.

## Post 5 — the sign flip

Alignment-faking reasoning — a model complying while privately disagreeing
— flips the sign: AUC 0.38–0.39. The deceptive reasoning is MORE consistent
across the panel than the honest kind.

And it's not giveaway words: redact the obvious cues, the flip stays
(AUC 0.39).

## Post 6 — where it's blind

Now the blindness:

• Instructed lies ("say X", X false): AUC 0.53, p=0.32. Nothing.
• Alignment-faking final OUTPUTS (not the reasoning): AUC 0.47 — a
marginal blip at best (p=0.045).

A detector that fired on falsehood would catch these. This one doesn't.
That's the clue.

## Post 7 — the story

The triangle score doesn't see false content. It sees reasoning that is
*organized by a strategy* — convincing, concealing, self-managing.

A lie you were told to tell isn't a strategy. You just say it. Nothing
about your thinking reorganizes — so nothing geometric changes.

## Post 8 — selectivity is the finding

We think the selectivity IS the result, not a limitation: it separates "the model is running a deception strategy" from "the output
happens to be false."

But it also means: this is NOT a lie detector. It misses overt lies
entirely, and one scenario reads inverted.

## Post 9 — the honest caveats (LONG)

Caveats:

• AUC 0.66 at best — far from deployable. This is evidence about structure,
not a product.
• Panel of three open 7–9B models; larger models untested.
• The sign flips by scenario — you cannot threshold this blindly without
knowing which regime you're in.
• Length-matching matters: raw AUCs run higher (e.g. 0.69 on insider
trading) and overstate the effect.
• "Deceptive" is defined by each dataset's labels — the machinery inherits
the quality of those labels.

## Post 10 — credit where due (LONG)

Lineage:

• Consistency catches liars — behaviorally: "How to Catch an AI Liar"
(@LPacchiardi et al.), consistency checks (Fluri, Paleka & Tramèr),
LM-vs-LM cross-examination
• Truth structure inside one model: Burns et al., Marks & Tegmark, "Truth
is Universal"
• Supervised deception probes hit 95–99% in-distribution: Apollo Research
(@MariusHobbhahn et al.)
• The sign-flip scenario: alignment faking — Greenblatt et al. (2024)
• Our translators are borrowed machinery: the model-stitching line (Lenc &
Vedaldi → Bansal et al. → Moschella et al. → Chen et al.)

Our piece: moving the consistency test from outputs to internal
representations, across a panel of models — and the selectivity that
falls out.
